title: Urban Green Spaces and City Parks
summary: Why cities plan parks and green spaces, how they improve air quality, lower temperatures, and support residents' wellbeing, and examples of green-space projects in Saudi cities like Riyadh and Jeddah.
poll: Cities should build more parks and green spaces, even if it costs a lot of money.

versions.title: Cities Need Green Spaces
versions.text:
Cities have many buildings and roads. But cities also need green spots. A park is a green spot with grass and trees.

People go to parks to rest. Kids play in parks. Parks have grass, trees, and paths. Some parks have ponds, too.

Parks are good for the air. Trees take in bad air. Trees give off fresh air. This helps people breathe.

Parks help in heat, too. A park with trees is cooler than hot streets. Shade from trees can cool a whole block.

Parks are good for how we feel, too. A walk in a park can calm your mind. Green plants can make people feel glad.

Saudi cities build new parks each year. You can help, too. Keep parks clean. Plant a tree if you can.

Parks are good for how people feel, too. A walk in a green park can calm a busy mind. Being near plants can make people feel happy and calm.

Cities in Saudi Arabia build new parks every year. You can help, too. Keep parks clean, and plant a tree if you can.

versions.title: Urban Green Spaces and City Parks
versions.text:
Cities are full of buildings, roads, and cars. But every growing city also needs green spaces. A park is a planned green space with grass and trees where people can relax and gather.

City planners design parks on purpose, because a crowded urban area needs places where families can rest. Parks have grass, trees, paths, and benches, and some parks even include ponds or small lakes for visitors to enjoy.

Parks improve the air we breathe. Trees take in dirty air and give off fresh oxygen, which helps keep the air in a busy city cleaner. This matters most in cities where pollution from cars and factories can build up.

Parks also help cool hot cities. A park full of trees is cooler than a street full of concrete, because shade and plants can lower the temperature of a whole neighborhood on a hot day.

Parks support wellbeing, too. A walk in a green park can calm a busy mind, and being near plants and grass can make people feel happier and calmer.

Saudi cities are building many new parks. In Riyadh, a large project called Green Riyadh aims to plant millions of new trees across the city. You can help, too: keep parks clean, and plant a tree if you can.

versions.title: Urban Green Spaces and City Parks
versions.text:
Cities are full of buildings, roads, and cars, yet every growing city also needs green spaces, because concrete alone cannot support a healthy, sustainable daily life. A park is a planned piece of urban infrastructure, a green space with grass and trees where people can relax and gather. Without enough parks, a fast-growing population can quickly feel the city's heat, noise, and crowding.

City planners design parks on purpose, because a crowded urban area needs places where families can rest and children can play safely within their own community. Parks have grass, trees, paths, and benches, and some parks even include ponds or small lakes that support local biodiversity, giving birds and small animals a place to live inside the city.

Parks improve the air we breathe. Trees take in dirty air and give off fresh oxygen, which helps keep the air in a busy city cleaner. This matters most in cities where pollution from cars and factories can steadily build up, affecting the health of everyone nearby, especially children and older residents.

Parks also help mitigate heat in hot cities. Streets and buildings made of concrete absorb heat during the day and release it at night, which scientists call the urban heat island effect, but a park full of trees stays noticeably cooler, because shade and plants can lower the temperature of a whole neighborhood on a hot day, sometimes by several degrees.

Parks support community wellbeing, too. A walk in a green park can calm a busy mind, and being near plants and grass can make people feel happier, calmer, and considerably less stressed.

Saudi cities are building many new parks as part of sustainable city planning. In Riyadh, a large project called Green Riyadh aims to plant millions of new trees and build many new parks across the entire city, while Jeddah has added green space along its long coastal waterfront. You can help, too: keep parks clean, and plant a tree if you can.

versions.title: Urban Green Spaces and City Parks
versions.text:
Cities are full of buildings, roads, and cars, yet every rapidly growing city also needs green spaces, because concrete alone cannot support a healthy, sustainable daily life over the long term, no matter how efficiently that concrete is arranged. A park is a planned piece of urban infrastructure, a green space with grass and trees where people can relax and gather. Without enough parks, a fast-growing population can quickly feel the city's heat, noise, and crowding.

City planners design parks deliberately, because a crowded urban area needs places where families can rest and children can play safely within their own community. Parks have grass, trees, paths, and benches, and some parks even include ponds or small lakes that support local biodiversity, giving birds and small animals a place to live inside an otherwise built-up city, often surprisingly close to busy roads and tall buildings.

This matters most in cities where pollution from cars and factories can steadily build up, affecting the health of everyone nearby, especially children and older residents who are more sensitive to poor air quality.

versions.title: Urban Green Spaces and City Parks
versions.text:
Cities are full of buildings, roads, and vehicles, yet every rapidly growing city also genuinely needs green spaces, because concrete alone cannot support a healthy, sustainable daily life over the long term, no matter how efficiently that concrete is arranged. A park is a deliberately planned piece of urban infrastructure, a green space with grass and trees where residents can relax and gather together. Without sufficient parks, a fast-growing population can quickly feel the city's heat, noise, and crowding more acutely than planners might originally anticipate.

City planners design parks quite deliberately, because a densely crowded urban area genuinely needs places where families can rest and children can play safely within their own surrounding community. Parks have grass, trees, paths, and benches, and some parks even include ponds or small lakes that support local biodiversity, giving birds and small animals a place to live inside an otherwise built-up urban environment, often surprisingly close to busy roads and tall buildings.

Parks substantially and measurably improve the air that city residents breathe every single day. Trees take in dirty, polluted air and give off fresh oxygen, which helps keep the air throughout a busy city considerably cleaner and genuinely healthier. This matters most in cities where pollution from vehicles and factories can steadily accumulate, seriously affecting the health of everyone nearby, especially children and older residents who remain more sensitive to poor air quality.

Parks also help meaningfully mitigate heat in increasingly hot cities. Streets and buildings constructed of concrete absorb considerable heat during the day and release it gradually at night, a phenomenon scientists formally call the urban heat island effect, but a park full of mature trees stays noticeably cooler, because shade and vegetation can meaningfully lower the temperature of an entire neighborhood on a sweltering day, sometimes by several degrees.

Parks genuinely support community wellbeing, too, in ways that researchers are still actively studying. A quiet walk in a green park can calm an otherwise busy mind, and being near plants and grass can make people feel considerably happier, calmer, and less stressed, according to numerous studies on urban life and mental health conducted around the world.

Saudi cities are actively building many new parks as part of sustainable, long-term urban planning. In Riyadh, an ambitious project called Green Riyadh aims to plant millions of new trees and build many new parks across the entire city, while Jeddah has added substantial new green space along its long coastal waterfront, genuinely benefiting residents and visitors alike. versions.title: Urban Green Spaces and City Parks
versions.text:
Cities are full of buildings, roads, and vehicles, yet every rapidly expanding city also genuinely and urgently needs green spaces, because concrete alone cannot adequately support a healthy, sustainable daily existence over the long term, regardless of how efficiently that concrete infrastructure is arranged. A park constitutes a deliberately planned piece of urban infrastructure, a green space with grass and trees where residents can relax and gather together communally. Without sufficient parks, a rapidly expanding population can quickly experience the city's accumulating heat, noise, and crowding far more acutely than municipal planners might originally have anticipated.

City planners design parks quite deliberately and systematically, because a densely crowded urban area genuinely requires places where families can rest comfortably and children can play safely within their own surrounding community. Parks characteristically include grass, trees, paths, and benches, and some parks even incorporate ponds or small lakes that actively support local biodiversity, providing birds and small animals a place to inhabit within an otherwise densely built-up urban environment, often surprisingly close to busy roads and towering buildings.

Parks substantially and measurably improve the air that city residents breathe every single day. Trees systematically absorb dirty, heavily polluted air and release fresh oxygen, which helps keep the air throughout an entire busy city considerably cleaner and genuinely healthier. This matters most significantly in cities where pollution from vehicles and industrial factories can steadily accumulate, seriously affecting the long-term health of everyone residing nearby, especially children and elderly residents who remain considerably more sensitive to poor air quality.

Parks also help meaningfully mitigate excessive heat in increasingly hot urban environments. Streets and buildings constructed predominantly of concrete absorb considerable heat throughout the day and release it gradually overnight, a well-documented phenomenon scientists formally term the urban heat island effect, but a park full of mature, established trees stays noticeably and measurably cooler, because shade and vegetation can meaningfully lower the ambient temperature of an entire neighborhood on a sweltering day, sometimes by several measurable degrees.

Parks genuinely support community wellbeing as well, in ways that researchers continue actively studying worldwide. A quiet, contemplative walk through a green park can meaningfully calm an otherwise busy, overstimulated mind, and being consistently near plants and grass can make people feel considerably happier, calmer, and substantially less stressed, according to numerous rigorous studies on urban life and mental health conducted across many different countries.

Saudi cities are actively and continuously building many new parks as part of sustainable, long-term urban planning initiatives. In Riyadh, an ambitious, large-scale project called Green Riyadh aims to plant millions upon millions of new trees and construct many new parks across the entire metropolitan city, while Jeddah has simultaneously added substantial new green space along its extensive coastal waterfront, genuinely benefiting both residents and visitors alike. You personally can meaningfully help as well, simply by consistently keeping parks clean and by planting a tree whenever you are genuinely able to do so.

keyWords.definition: the basic structures and systems, such as roads, parks, and buildings, that a city needs to function
keyWords.example: The city invested heavily in new transportation infrastructure.

keyWords.definition: to make a problem less severe or harmful
keyWords.example: Planting trees can help mitigate the effects of extreme heat.

keyWords.definition: a group of people who live in the same area and share common interests
keyWords.example: The whole community gathered to clean up the local park.

questions.stem: Which sentence best summarizes the article?
options: Parks exist only for recreational sports.
Concrete always keeps cities cooler than trees do.

Cities deliberately plan parks as green infrastructure to fight pollution and heat while supporting community wellbeing, and Saudi cities are expanding this effort through sustainable projects like Green Riyadh.
Biodiversity has no connection to city parks.
questions.why: The article explains why cities plan parks, their environmental and wellbeing benefits, and real Saudi examples like Green Riyadh.

wrong.A: The article describes many benefits beyond sports.
wrong.B: The article says trees keep areas cooler than concrete, not the reverse.
wrong.D: The article connects parks to supporting local biodiversity.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is the urban heat island effect?
options: A type of park built only on islands.
A scientific name for city parks.
A method for cooling buildings with ice.
Concrete streets and buildings absorb heat during the day and release it at night, keeping cities hotter.
questions.why: The article defines the urban heat island effect as concrete absorbing heat during the day and releasing it at night.

wrong.B: Parks are described as cooler, not as the heat island effect itself.

questions.stem: What does the Green Riyadh project aim to do, according to the article?
options: Remove public parks to build more highways.
Plant millions of new trees and build many new parks across the city.
Replace all green spaces with shopping centers.
Limit the number of residents allowed inside the city to a very small fixed number.
questions.why: The article states that Green Riyadh aims to plant millions of new trees and build new parks across the city.

wrong.A: The project adds green space; it does not remove parks.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why parks support local biodiversity?
options: Ponds and green spaces give birds and small animals a place to live within the city.
Animals avoid cities altogether.
Parks are built entirely underwater.
Parks have no plants or water features anywhere inside them at all, according to critics.
questions.why: The article explains that ponds and small lakes in parks give birds and small animals a place to live inside the city.

wrong.B: The article shows animals do live in cities, within parks.
wrong.D: Parks are described as including plants and water features.

questions.stem: Why might older residents benefit the most from cleaner air in parks?
options: They never leave their own homes for any reason throughout the entire year.
They dislike green spaces.
They are immune to pollution.
They are described as more sensitive to poor air quality.
questions.why: The article explains that older residents are more sensitive to poor air quality, so cleaner air from parks benefits them especially.

wrong.A: The article does not say older residents never leave home.
wrong.B: Disliking green spaces is not mentioned.
wrong.C: The article says the opposite: older residents are more sensitive to pollution.

questions.stem: In the article, what does mitigate mean?
options: To make a problem considerably worse than it originally was before
To lessen or reduce the severity of a problem
To completely ignore a problem
To create a brand-new problem
questions.why: The article uses mitigate to describe how parks help lessen the severity of heat in cities.

wrong.A: Mitigate means to reduce, not worsen, a problem.
wrong.C: Mitigate involves addressing a problem, not ignoring it.
wrong.D: Mitigate does not mean creating a new problem.

questions.stem: How does the article structure its explanation of urban parks?
options: It argues that parks should be removed from all cities.
It presents examples before ever explaining any benefits.
It explains why cities plan parks, then their environmental and wellbeing benefits, then real examples of green-space projects in Saudi cities.
It focuses only on one single park in one single city.
questions.why: The article first explains why parks are planned, then describes benefits such as air quality and heat mitigation, then gives examples like Green Riyadh and Jeddah's waterfront.

wrong.A: The article supports building more parks, not removing them.
wrong.B: Benefits are explained before most of the examples.
wrong.D: The article mentions more than one city and project.

questions.stem: Why does a park full of mature trees stay cooler than a street full of concrete?
options: Shade and vegetation lower the temperature, while concrete absorbs and slowly releases heat.
Parks are built below ground, away from the sun.
Concrete reflects all sunlight back into space.
Trees generate their own artificial cooling systems.
questions.why: The article explains that shade and vegetation lower temperatures, while concrete absorbs heat during the day and releases it at night.

wrong.B: Parks are not built below ground.
wrong.C: The article does not describe concrete reflecting sunlight into space.
wrong.D: Trees do not have artificial cooling systems.

HIGH.prompt: Why do you think city planners in Saudi Arabia are investing in projects like Green Riyadh? Make a claim and support it with evidence from the article.
checklist: I made a clear claim about why planners invest in green-space projects.
I supported my claim with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained my reasoning and used correct grammar and punctuation.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think city planners in Saudi Arabia are investing in projects like Green Riyadh because green spaces provide real, lasting benefits to residents. The article explains that parks help mitigate the urban heat island effect, since shade and vegetation can lower a neighborhood's temperature on a hot day, and that trees also improve air quality by absorbing pollution and releasing oxygen. Beyond these environmental benefits, parks support community wellbeing by giving people a calm place to walk and relax, which suggests that these projects are a long-term investment in both the environment and public health.
